parole.testo: Inherited from Old Church Slavonic -ачь (-ačĭ) and -чь (-čĭ).

parole.significato: Forms masculine nouns denoting a person associated with a field of study, profession, or characteristic.
parole.testo: For native terms, inherited from Old Church Slavonic -икъ (-ikŭ), from Proto-Slavic *-ikъ. Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *-kos Proto-Hellenic *-kos Ancient Greek -κός (-kós) Ancient Greek -ικός (-ikós)der. Proto-Indo-European *-ikos Proto-Italic *-ikos Latin -icusder. Bulgarian -ик For borrowin
Derived from Latin -ere or -īre. Ultimately from Latin infinitive endings -ere, -īre, whence Italian -ire, French -ir, German -ieren, + native a-conjugation endings.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek -ία (-ía), -εια (-eia), and -εῖον (-eîon), found in loanwords.

parole.significato: Forms diminutives of feminine nouns, including personal names
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Church Slavonic -ъка (-ŭka) and -ька (-ĭka) (the latter causes palatalization of preceding velars).

parole.significato: Forms diminutive forms of masculine nouns (including personal names)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ъko and *-ьko (the later causing palatalization of preceding velars).

parole.significato: Used to form compound words. Usually excrescent.
parole.testo: For native terms, inherited from Old Church Slavonic -о- (-o-), from Proto-Slavic *-o-. Etymology tree Ancient Greek -ο- (-o-)der. Latin -o-bor. Bulgarian -о- For borrowings, borrowed from Latin -o-, from Ancient Greek -ο- (-o-).

parole.significato: abstraction (hiding implementation details from the interface of a component, to decrease complexity through interdepen…
parole.testo: Borrowed via Russian абстра́кция (abstrákcija) and German Abstraktion, from Late Latin abstractiō.

parole.significato: acquisition of something without effort, or undeservingly; a bargain, steal
parole.testo: From either Turkish avanta or Greek αβάντα (avánta), from Old Italian avantare, avanti or avante.
Borrowed from Italian avaria and Greek αβαρία (avaría).
Borrowed from Russian а́вто- (ávto-), German auto-, and Ancient Greek αὐτός (autós). Senses 1 and 2 are derived from Ancient Greek, while the automotive sense is borrowed through German or Russian.

parole.significato: male lawyer, advocate, attorney, counsel, pleader, barrister, solicitor
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Advokat and Russian адвока́т (advokát).

From Russian адмира́л (admirál) and German Admiral, from English and Old French admiral, from Medieval Latin admiralis, from Arabic أَمِير (ʔamīr, “commander”) + -alis (“-al”) under influence from admīrārī (“to admire, to respect”).
Borrowed from French académie, German Akademie, and Russian акаде́мия (akadémija).

parole.significato: accordion, squeezebox (a small, portable, keyed wind instrument)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French accordéon or Russian аккордео́н (akkordeón).
Borrowed from French à la or Italian alla.
Borrowed from Romanian album or German Album; each ultimately from Latin album (“blank white writing tablet”), from Latin albus (“white”).
Borrowed from French ambulatoire or Russian амбулато́рия (ambulatórija).

parole.significato: anaconda (any of various large nonvenomous snake of the genus Eunectes)
parole.testo: Internationalism, possibly borrowed from French anaconda or Spanish anaconda, ultimately from Sinhalese හෙනකඳයා (henakaⁿdayā, “whip snake”), from හෙන (hena, “lightning, thunderbolt”) + කඳ (kaⁿda, “stem, trunk, body”) or from Tamil ஆனைக்கொன்றான் (āṉaikkoṉṟāṉ, “having killed an elephant”), from ஆனை (ā
Borrowed from German Archiv or Russian архи́в (arxív).
Borrowed from Russian а́стма (ástma) or German Asthma.
Borrowed from either Russian атом (atom), German Atom or French atome; from Latin atomus (“smallest particle”), from Ancient Greek ἄτομος (átomos).
Borrowed from French bal or German Ball.

parole.significato: balcony (enclosed platform, projecting outwards from the floor of a building)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French balcon or Italian balcone.
Borrowed from French banane or Portuguese banana.

parole.significato: banquet, feast, gala (formal lunch or dinner, usually in honor of someone or an event)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Bankett or Russian банке́т (bankét). Morphologically parsable as ба́нка (bánka) + -ет (-et).

Inherited from Middle Bulgarian бирь (birĭ) (attested in Manasses Chronicle). Further origin disputed. Either: * Deverbal from the intensive stem *birati of native бера́ (berá, “to pick”). * Of Oghur origin, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *bẹ̄ri.

Either: * Contracted from an earlier *bodьcь, a diminutive of Proto-Slavic *bodъ (“piercing”); * Deverbal from бо́цам (bócam, “to poke, to jolt”), factitive from Proto-Slavic *bokъ (“protrusion”) or *bosti (“to pierce”).

Attested as Middle Bulgarian боубрегъ (bubregŭ), боубрѣгъ (bubrěgŭ) in late Church Slavonic texts. Either borrowed from Ottoman Turkish بوبرك (böbrek) or less likely of Oghur origin, in view of the voiced reflex of proto-Turkic *-ek, which is even more common in Macedonian бубрег (bubreg), Serbo-Cro
From either German Vakuum or French vacuum, ultimately from Latin vacuum (adjective, neuter of vacuus (“empty”)).

Inherited from Old Church Slavonic ватахъ (vataxŭ, “chief, commander”). Probably of Oghur origin, related to dialectal Bulgarian ватог (vatog, “hearth”). Alternatively, according to Vl. Georgiev (BER): a Thracian borrowing, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wedʰ- (“to lead”).

Borrowed either directly from Tosk Albanian vatër, or from Romanian vatră or Aromanian vatrã, which in turn are borrowed from Tosk Albanian vatër (definite form vatra), from Proto-Albanian *ōtar, obtained through the *o to *vo-/*va- development which is observed exclusively in the Albanian language
Ultimately from Latin vīrus (“poison”), borrowed from some intermediate Western language (probably German Virus) or from Russian ви́рус (vírus).
Calque of French haut-parleur or German Lautsprecher. By surface analysis, висо̀к (visòk) + -о- (-o-) + говори́тел (govorítel).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *vòrgъ or *vьragъ (with fixed accentuation).

parole.significato: nut (a piece of hardware, typically metal and typically hexagonal or square in shape, with a hole through it having int…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian га́йка (gájka), from Proto-Slavic *gajьka. Further origin is uncertain: * Either related to Bulgarian жир (žir, “fat, grease”), гоя́ (gojá, “to lush”) with initial meaning something that fastens, fixates (compare Ukrainian га́їти (hájity, “to hinder one's motion”), Czech hájit
Borrowed from French graphite, German Graphit, or Russian графи́т (grafít).

parole.significato: sin, violation of sacred norms or laws
parole.testo: Semantic loan from Ancient Greek ἁμαρτία (hamartía, “error, mistake; guilt, sin”), ἁμαρτάνω (hamartánō, “to miss; to fail, sin”), Latin peccāre (“to trip, stumble; to transgress”), or peccātum (“error, mistake, deficiency; sin”).
Borrowed from French gomme and German Gummi.
Probably cognate with Serbo-Croatian гу̏та (“edema”), Slovene guta (“apoplexy”), either from Proto-Slavic *guta (Georgiev, Sławski) or borrowed from Latin gutta (“drop”) (Snoj).
According to BER, borrowed from either German Diagnose, French diagnose or Russian диа́гноз (diágnoz), ultimately from Ancient Greek διάγνωσις (diágnōsis).
Borrowed from German Doktor, Polish doktor, or Russian до́ктор (dóktor).

parole.significato: tomato (a widely cultivated plant, Solanum lycopersicum, having edible fruit)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish طوماتس (domates) or Greek ντομάτα (ntomáta).
Borrowed from Greek ντουζίνα (ntouzína), from Neapolitan duzzina, either from Occitan dotzena or French douzaine (or the corresponding ancestor languages), ultimately from Latin duodecim.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *duma (“thought”), Origin disputed. Either from Germanic, from Proto-Germanic *dōmaz (“judicial decision, act, thought”). Or from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewh₂- (“to smoke”), akin to Proto-Slavic *duti (“to blow, to inflate”), Proto-Slavic *dymъ (“smoke”).
Borrowed from Russian эне́ргия (enérgija) and German Energie. First attested in 1871.

Either from Russian эпило́г (epilóg) (borrowed from French) or directly from French épilogue; both from Latin epilogus from Ancient Greek ἐπῐ́λογος (epĭ́logos, “epilogue of a play, peroration of a speech"”).

parole.significato: dowry (gift presented to a newlywed family by the bride's kin)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Romanian zestre, from Latin dextrae pl. According to Stefan Mladenov, the Bulgarian and Romanian terms may alternatively stem from Proto-Slavic *zęt- (“kinship”) + *-tra, though this is very unlikely.
Borrowed from German instinktiv + -ен (-en), or from Russian инстинкти́вный (instinktívnyj).

parole.significato: inflation (increase in the quantity of money, leading to a devaluation of existing money, adjusted for by way of higher…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French inflation or German Inflation.

parole.significato: iodine (a chemical element (symbol: I) with an atomic number of 53; one of the halogens)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French iode, German Jod, or Russian йод (jod). First attested in 1870.
Borrowed from German Kabel or Russian ка́бель (kábelʹ).
Either from Greek καίω (kaío, “to burn”) and αυγά (avgá, “eggs”) or borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قایغنه (kayğana), from Classical Persian خاگینه (xāgīna). Compare Serbo-Croatian ка̏јгана /kȁjgana.
Borrowed from Russian ка́ктус (káktus) or Latin cactus.

parole.significato: compartment, camera (closed empty space with a special purpose in devices, machines, apparatuses)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Kammer or Russian ка́мера (kámera).
Either from Greek κάμινος (káminos, “furnace”) (from the same term in Ancient Greek), or from Latin (camera) camīnāta (“heated (room/chamber)”), whence also Albanian kaminë.
Of Thracian or Dacian origin (see the etymology of Carpathian mountains). Cognate with Macedonian карпа (karpa). Alternatively, from Albanian karpë.
Borrowed from French constitution, German Konstitution, or Russian конститу́ция (konstitúcija). First attested in 1843.
Borrowed from Latin corōna, either via Greek κορώνα (koróna) or Russian корона (korona).
Borrowed from either German Xenon, French xénon or Russian ксено́н (ksenón), from Ancient Greek ξένον (xénon), neuter of ξένος (xénos, “foreign, strange”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kury (v-stem) and *kurъve. By surface analysis, кур (kur, “rooster, cock”) + -ва (-va).

parole.significato: a type of jug or pitcher (an instrument for drinking)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Church Slavonic кръчагъ (krŭčagŭ), of disputed origin: * Possibly a native derivation, from къ́ркам (kắrkam, “to swill”) + -аг (-ag). Favoured by Mladenov. * Alternatively, of Oghur origin akin to Hungarian korsó (“jug”). Borrowed into Albanian kërçak.

Unclear. If native, then probably inherited from Proto-Slavic *ťutati (“to keep an eye on”). Alternatively: * M. Filipova-Bajrova: Borrowed from Greek κοίτομαι (koítomai, “to lie down”). * Mladenov: Influenced by Ottoman Turkish كوذماك (güdmek, “to graze, await”), via semantic shift “to graze → to t
Borrowed either from Russian леопард (leopard) or German Leopard, from Latin leopardus, from Ancient Greek λεόπαρδος (leópardos).
Borrowed from Greek λεμόνι (lemóni) or Ottoman Turkish لیمون (limon).

* Back-formed (with stress retraction) from the diminutive луни́ца (luníca, “small moon”) of Etymology 1. * Derived from the word луна́ (luná, “moon”) with stress retraction. * Borrowed from Romanian alunea (“hazelnut”) under the impression that it is a collective noun, similarly to нивя́ (nivjá, “f

parole.significato: magnate, tycoon (a wealthy and influential person, especially in business)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Magnat or Russian магна́т (magnát). First attested in 1871.

parole.significato: mother (a female parent, especially of a human; a female who parents a child (which she has given birth to, adopted, fo…
parole.testo: Either as a diminutive form of Proto-Slavic *mati through Old Church Slavonic мати (mati) or from the unattested form in Proto-Slavic *matьka, which through anticipation of the palatalization became the Proto-Slavic *majtka and later through assimilation the /t/ was dropped.

parole.significato: major (military rank between captain and lieutenant colonel, or a person who holds such a rank)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian майо́р (majór) and German Major, from Latin maior.
Borrowed from French médaille or Russian меда́ль (medálʹ).
From French millionnaire, via Russian миллионе́р (millionér); or, alternatively, via archaic Romanian milioner.
Ultimately from Ancient Greek μυριάς (muriás), borrowed either from French myriade or German Myriade.
Borrowed from French meeting or Russian ми́тинг (míting). First attested in the 14th of March 1853. The ultimate stress of the word is due to how it is pronounced in French.

parole.significato: short church service to offer prayer, give thanks or mark a special occasion
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian моле́бен (molében), or from Old Church Slavonic мольбьнъ (molĭbĭnŭ).
Borrowed from French nègre or Russian негр (negr). First attested in 1869.
Borrowed either from French nitrate or German Nitrat. Internationalism, part of the international scientific vocabulary.
Ultimately from Latin nōrmālis, either via French normal or Russian норма́льный (normálʹnyj).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ovьsiga or *ovisika. By surface analysis, ове́с (ovés) + -ига (-iga).
Borrowed from Russian офице́р (oficér), either directly from German Offizier from Latin officiārius (“officer”), or first via Polish oficer.

Possibly borrowed from Austrian German Palatschinke (reformed with Slavic suffix -inka) or Hungarian palacsinta (reformed with Slavic suffix -inka). Cognate with Czech palačinka, Serbo-Croatian палачинка and Slovak palacinka.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek πῠ́ργος (pŭ́rgos, “watchtower”), probably of Ancient Macedonian (or alternatively Pelasgian) origin, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰergʰ- (“to tower”).
Borrowed from English port or from German Port, ultimately from Latin portus.

parole.significato: post, position, office (appointed position in an organization; job)
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from French poste. Alternatively from Ottoman Turkish پوست (post, “position, office”) or Romanian post (“post, position, job”). First attested in 1849.
Ultimately from Latin prō centum (“per hundred”), via German Prozent or possibly Russian проце́нт (procént).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *pročь, *pročii, and *proče. Comparative forms of *prokъ.

parole.significato: rose (garden plant of the genus Rosa, a thorny shrub)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French rose or Russian ро́за (róza).
Borrowed from German Seminar or Russian семина́р (seminár).
Borrowed from French sérénade or Italian serenata.

parole.significato: symphony (an extended piece of music of sophisticated structure)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian симфо́ния (simfónija) or German Symphonie.

parole.significato: skeleton (the system that provides support to an organism, where in vertebrates it is internal and consists of bones an…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French squelette, German Skelett, Russian скелет (skelet), or Greek σκελετός (skeletós).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *skǫdьlъ, either borrowed from Latin scandula (“shingle”) or cognate with it.
From Proto-Slavic *slědъ m, with diachronic gender shift, or possibly an action noun from the respective causative verb Proto-Slavic *slěditi (“to trace”).
Borrowed from French soupe or Greek σούπα (soúpa). First attested in 1835. Cognate with Bulgarian съ́рбам (sắrbam, “slurp”).

Continues Old Church Slavonic соуръ (surŭ), probably of Oghur or Kipchak (Cuman) origin cognate with Kazakh сұр (sur, “gray”) (possibly from Proto-Turkic *sǖr- (“to vade away”)) or from an o-grade of Proto-Slavic *syrъ (“raw, damp”).

Either augmentative of Proto-Slavic *xala (“worn-out cloth”) + -ище (-ište) or borrowed from Ottoman Turkish خالیجه (halıca, “carpet”) (whence Turkish haliçe, Azerbaijani xalça). Cognate with Macedonian алишта pl (ališta).

parole.significato: unionist (a supporter of a political union)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French unioniste or English unionist.
